item.title: Spontaneous mechanical patterning in active elastic tissues with stress feedback
item.description: arXiv:2611.14943v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The active mechanics of biological tissues is often governed by embedded active contractile fibers responding to mechanical feedback. We introduce a minimal model of a solid-like tissue where the mechanics is controlled by feedback of local active and elastic stresses on fiber organization. The resulting tissue generically exhibits a bistable response to external strain and spontaneously segregates into domains of orthogonally aligned fibers. Our theory thus provides a minimal mechanical feedback mechanism generating orthogonal structural alignment ubiquitous in biological tissues.
item.dc:creator: Henrik Weyer, Divyoj Singh, M. Cristina Marchetti

item.title: Feedback-induced mechanical bistability and perpendicular-domain formation in active elastic tissues
item.description: arXiv:2611.14964v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Contractile fibers in muscle tissues are highly aligned over the scale of many cells. Muscle layers surrounding organs with an inner lumen are often arranged in orthogonal directions. Here, we study a minimal mechanism of how structural order and its patterning into orthogonally aligned domains can emerge from mechanical feedback alone. The central idea is that contractile fibers align in the direction of the local active and elastic stresses, a feedback motivated by the maturation of muscle fibers under tension. We thus model muscle tissue as an active nematic solid with stress feedback: an elastic medium with embedded contractile fibers that are reinforced along the directions of the local tissue stresses. We find that the feedback from the contractile fiber stress is self-amplifying and drives spontaneous fiber alignment. Feedback from the elastic stress couples the alignment to the mechanical boundary conditions and tissue geometry. Depending on the mechanical boundary conditions, the elastic-stress feedback stabilizes two orthogonally aligned tissue states, resulting in a structurally and mechanically bistable tissue that shows a hysteretic stress-strain response. In spatially extended tissues, this bistability gives rise to orthogonally aligned domains separated by domain walls. In an annulus surrounding a pressurized lumen, a radially aligned inner domain and a circumferentially aligned outer domain stably coexist because the domain wall is pinned at a position that results in the fibers carrying the lumen pressure. Our results show that stress feedback can pattern structural order by coupling spontaneous alignment to the tissue geometry. Our mechanism thus provides a purely mechanical route to orthogonal fiber patterning in muscle tissues.
item.dc:creator: Divyoj Singh, Henrik Weyer, Harry Kroft, M. Cristina Marchetti

item.title: A unified finite-site framework for scaffold-client biocondensation
item.description: arXiv:2611.15007v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Client recruitment into biomolecular condensates does not determine how stronger binding changes the bulk free-energy advantage of demixing. Here, we use a unified finite-site thermodynamic framework to examine how scaffold-client interactions affect both the response of a fixed-composition mixture and the organization of its ternary phase diagram. The thermodynamic response to increasing client affinity is determined by the difference in heterotypic bonding between the complete equilibrium phase-separated sample and the corresponding homogeneous state. A finite region of the model exhibits positive scaffold-client concentration covariance but negative heterotypic bond contrast: stronger binding reduces the demixing advantage even when both species enrich in the dense phase. This reduction also occurs with independent scaffold self-association and client-binding site pools, without direct displacement of scaffold bonds. A negative response does not by itself imply condensate shrinkage or dissolution. Across composition space, the same finite binding constraints support scaffold-rich and heterotypic coexistence regimes with distinct bond populations. For divalent clients, these regimes can occupy disconnected regions of the phase diagram and reconnect upon increasing client affinity, depending on scaffold cohesion. Critical-point continuation identifies the folds and cusp organizing these changes, while client valence restricts the parameter range over which disconnected coexistence occurs. Explicit-particle Monte Carlo simulations reproduce the qualitative reentrant response and provide finite-size evidence for disconnected coexistence. These results provide a bond-resolved characterization of fixed-parent affinity response and a complementary description of coexistence under specified association constraints.
item.dc:creator: Hamza Coban, Alfredo Alexander-Katz

item.title: Proliferating against the current: how multistep branching nucleation can sort microtubule polarity in the spindle
item.description: arXiv:2611.16200v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The spindle, which segregates chromosomes during cell division, is a paradigm of cytoskeletal self-organization: a highly ordered structure that persists for hours is assembled from dynamic microtubules that branch, grow, slide, and turn over within tens of seconds. Its microtubules point inward, with minus ends clustered at the poles and plus ends extending toward the chromosomes at the center of the structure. In large meiotic spindles this arrangement is puzzling, since microtubules nucleate near the chromosomes and grow at their plus ends much faster than motors slide them backward. One would therefore expect the plus ends, rather than the minus ends, to radiate outward. Here, we propose a resolution to this seeming paradox through a kinetic model that integrates the core filament-level processes. When branching complexes assemble with a sufficient delay, for instance through several sequential rate-limiting steps, they accumulate on old microtubule lattice sites near the backward-sliding minus ends of mother microtubules. Each generation is then born farther back than the last, so the self-renewing population drifts toward the minus ends even though each filament's center advances toward its plus end. For the sliding and growth velocities measured in Xenopus egg extract spindles, a multistep mechanism requires at least four rate-limiting steps. The kinetic theory has a surprisingly amenable structure: the filament length configuration variable can be eliminated exactly, yielding a finite space-time hierarchy, and the direction of population drift follows from a general criterion comparing the mean lattice age at branching sites with the ratio of plus-end advance to sliding speed.
item.dc:creator: Ido Lavi, Sebastian F\"urthauer, Daniel J. Needleman, Michael J. Shelley

item.title: Stretched bilayer-cytoskeleton links hold echinocytes in a model splenic slit
item.description: arXiv:2611.16241v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Stored red blood cells become echinocytes, growing spicules before losing membrane; the spleen clears the resulting small, spherical cells. Whether spicules alone hinder splenic passage is unknown. Shape and area change together. In a two-component model whose shrinking cytoskeleton raises spicules, we drove a discocyte and stage I to III echinocytes of equal area and volume through a model splenic slit. The pressure drop needed to pass rose with stage; stage III echinocytes were held at 37 to 50 times the pressure drop that passed the discocyte. Bilayer-cytoskeleton links stretched near full extension held these cells; lengthening them about twofold released a held cell. Capillary-sized channels, as in our device, separated the stages far less. Of the shape classes in stored blood, the model held at high pressure drops only storage-induced microerythrocytes, which perfused human spleens clear most. Spicules, besides membrane loss, may decide which stored cells the spleen retains.
item.dc:creator: Zhaojie Chai, Jianlu Zheng, He Li, Ming Dao, George Em Karniadakis

item.title: Optimal Driving between Nonequilibrium Steady States under a Dissipation Budget
item.description: arXiv:2611.14891v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Driving between nonequilibrium steady states incurs two thermodynamic costs: excess entropy production (EP) resulting from changing control parameters, and housekeeping EP required to sustain steady currents. Conventional fixed-duration optimization minimizes the former while neglecting the latter. Here, we instead optimize excess EP over both the protocol and its duration subject to a fixed leading order of housekeeping-EP budget, thereby minimizing total EP for that budget constraint. In the slow-driving regime, accumulated housekeeping EP acts as an entropic time, mapping the problem to a geodesic optimization under a friction metric weighted by the steady-state EP rate. This resource-based geometry determines optimal paths and schedules for systems that continue to dissipate even in steady states, establishing an intrinsic trade-off between housekeeping and excess EPs. Near equilibrium, this framework further yields geometric lower bounds on total EP, attained with equipartition at the optimal budget given by a modified thermodynamic length. Numerical simulations of a three-state model for an ATP-driven calcium pump reveal distinct optimal protocols compared to fixed-duration driving, confirming the total-EP bounds.
item.dc:creator: Keisuke Sugie, Dimitri Loutchko, Tetsuya J. Kobayashi

item.title: Thermal convection and jets produced by human exhalation dominate the indoor spreading of emitted CO$_2$ and aerosols
item.description: arXiv:2611.15791v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: For understanding airborne viral infection pathways, the prediction of the spreading and effective diffusivity of saliva droplets emitted from a person while speaking and breathing is crucial. In non-ventilated indoor spaces, the spreading of tracer particles or molecules emitted by a person is governed by the complex interplay of molecular diffusion, convection due to body heat and temperature boundary conditions as well as propulsion due to breathing in and out. By comparison of grid-based simulations of the compressible Navier-Stokes equation with experiments measuring the spreading of CO$_2$ emitted from a person, we demonstrate that molecular diffusion of CO$_2$ is present, but that the long-distance CO$_2$ spreading is completely dominated by the combination of convection due to body heat and temperature gradients at walls and windows and the periodic breathing pattern of a person. Breathing out induces long-range advection by a mid-Reynolds number flow pattern akin to the Landau-Squire jet, while breathing in creates only short-range flow. In conjunction with thermal convection, this symmetry breaking between breathing in and out produces fast long-distance transport of CO$_2$ and small aerosols.
item.dc:creator: Lars A. Natusch, Roland R. Netz

item.title: Silscore: modelling siRNA potency with positional thermodynamics and data-selected nucleotide-identity terms
item.description: arXiv:2611.15812v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) enable programmable gene silencing, but candidates targeting the same transcript can differ markedly in potency. Existing predictors range from interpretable empirical rules with limited accuracy to high-capacity models that can lose performance when datasets or targets change. We present Silscore, a guide-only model that combines a quadratic preference for overall duplex stability, a position-resolved profile of nearest-neighbour stacking energies and sparse nucleotide-identity terms selected from residuals left unexplained by thermodynamics. Its main fit uses 26 parameters, fewer than half as many as any trainable comparator evaluated here. We evaluate Silscore on the canonical split of the Huesken dataset, two external datasets (Mixset and Katoh-Suzuki), and an evaluation in which the same guides are tested after training on dissimilar targets. Silscore attains the highest observed Pearson correlation in all three transfer evaluations, and the data support an advantage over every applicable comparator on Katoh-Suzuki. For a fixed evaluation set, we compare two equally sized training sets with higher or lower sequence similarity to the evaluation sequences. After training on the less similar sequences, Silscore has the highest observed correlation, and the data do not establish a change in its performance. The fitted parameters can also be interpreted directly: identity terms locate sequence effects that base-pairing energies cannot express, global stability has a data-estimated intermediate optimum, and local energy profiles recover terminal asymmetry and a preference for weaker seed and stronger central pairing. Silscore thus provides a compact, data-driven model that combines strong predictive performance with robustness when tested in new settings and expresses previously reported empirical preferences as quantities estimated from data.
item.dc:creator: Giuseppe Sacco, Isabella Baldini, Riccardo Paone, Mattia Capulli, Guido Sanguinetti, Giovanni Bussi

item.title: Interactions from memory footprints: Cage-hopping, mnemotaxis & nonreciprocity
item.description: arXiv:2611.17257v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Cellular motility is integral to biological processes ranging from foraging to immune responses and cancer metastasis. While cells often navigate by sensing pre-existing environmental cues, many actively steer their future trajectories by remodeling their surroundings via shared, long-lived physicochemical trails called memory footprints. These stigmergic responses to shared footprints also influence large-scale self-organization, such as the early stages of microcolony formation. Despite recent progress, a unified framework connecting single-cell dynamics and collective organization through effective pairwise interactions remains elusive. To bridge this gap, we perform extensive agent-based simulations of an interacting random walk model that explicitly accounts for footprint deposition and decay. Our approach reveals distinct cage-hopping dynamics in solitary cells, as well as complex mnemotactic responses to externally imposed memory gradients. Furthermore, we demonstrate that shared spatial memory fields generate nontrivial effective pairwise interactions, both reciprocal and nonreciprocal, that shape the collective organization of cell populations. Beyond multiscale cellular dynamics, our findings have broader implications for the collective behavior of synthetic active matter, such as swarm robots.
item.dc:creator: Jyoti Prasad Banerjee, Sambodh Sinha, Shashi Thutupalli, Rituparno Mandal, Deb Sankar Banerjee

item.title: Confinement Limits Cell Shape and Mitotic Pressure During Division
item.description: arXiv:2602.18909v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Cells often divide under mechanical confinement, where surrounding structures restrict shape changes during cytokinesis. We analyze a minimal model of a dividing cell as an incompressible volume bounded by an interface with effective isotropic tension, and show that confinement imposes a minimum attainable furrow radius. Beyond this limit, the cytokinetic ring can continue to contract within a septum without further furrow ingression, leaving the cell shape, mitotic pressure, and transmitted force unchanged. We determine this confinement-limited state for rigid parallel walls, soft axial confinement, and three-dimensional enclosures. Between parallel walls, the limiting force and minimum furrow radius collapse onto universal curves when scaled by surface tension and cell size. In soft confinement, environmental stiffness and spindle forces select the operating point. In three-dimensional confinement, the free volume between the cell and the confinement controls force transmission and cell shape. This yields a method for inferring the mechanical state of a cell dividing in deformable three-dimensional confinement from its shape. The radius and tangent angle of the cell surface at the stalled furrow and at the point where the cell detaches from its surroundings determine the mitotic pressure and the axial force carried by the cell surface, relative to the cortical tension.
item.dc:creator: Amit Singh Vishen

item.title: Exact Fixed-Point Constraints in Neural-ODEs: Injecting Prior Knowledge into the Network Parameters
item.description: arXiv:2605.10613v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Neural ordinary differential equations (Neural-ODEs) learn a velocity field from data. Often, however, additional information on the target field is available, such as the location of some of its equilibria or, more generally, its values at given points. We introduce a method to inject this information directly into the parameters of a Neural-ODE, so that a finite set of prescribed fixed points holds exactly throughout training, with no penalty terms and no post-hoc projection. The output matrix is parametrized through the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse, implemented by a thin QR factorization of the hidden features at the prescribed points. This splits the output matrix into a component determined by the constraints and a free one, which shapes the field away from the prescribed points without altering its values there. As a result, the constrained Neural-ODE remains a universal approximator of the continuous vector fields compatible with the constraints. We test the method on a two-dimensional Lotka-Volterra competition model with four equilibria. In vector field regression, the constrained model keeps the fixed-point residual at single-precision round-off, and its test error is up to about five times lower than that of an unconstrained network of the same architecture. A soft penalty on the equilibria lowers the residual only at the cost of accuracy, and still leaves it at least an order of magnitude above that of the constrained model. Trained to convergence on datasets of increasing size, the unconstrained and penalized networks saturate already on small datasets, while the constrained model keeps improving over a wider range. Close to the equilibria and over long time horizons, the constrained model is the most accurate at every dataset size considered. This also holds when the models are trained on observed trajectories, by backpropagation through the ODE solver.
item.dc:creator: Feliciano Giuseppe Pacifico, Duccio Fanelli, Lorenzo Buffoni, Lorenzo Chicchi, Diego Febbe, Raffaele Marino

item.title: Local molecular motions encode time-resolved infrared spectra of proteins
item.description: arXiv:2608.12914v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Time-resolved infrared spectroscopy probes protein dynamics over timescales spanning more than ten orders of magnitude, yet the molecular motions underlying the observed kinetic signatures have remained elusive. Here we combine transient infrared spectroscopy with nonequilibrium molecular dynamics simulations to establish a direct connection between experimental relaxation times and local structural motions. Studying single-domain allosteric proteins, we find that inter-residue contact distances provide the structural representation that most faithfully reproduces the experimental dynamics. Correlation analysis identifies localized networks of coordinated contacts that mediate long-range coupling between secondary-structure elements. The characteristic timescales of these contact networks quantitatively match the experimentally observed relaxation processes, enabling each kinetic step to be assigned to a specific molecular motion. Applied to allosteric signal propagation in PDZ3 and photoinduced perturbation of the binding pocket of PDZ2 or a ligand binding to PDZ2, this framework provides an atomistic picture of hierarchical protein relaxation and establishes a general framework for connecting transient infrared spectroscopy with the molecular mechanisms of protein dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Emanuel Dorbath, Peter Hamm, Gerhard Stock

item.title: Simultaneous measurements of enzyme propagation and biopolymer mobility elucidate the directional degradation of a dense biopolymer matrix
item.description: arXiv:2609.03792v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Enzymatic degradation of dense biopolymer matrices is central to natural processes like digestion and cancer progression, as well as applications in biomedicine, biomass valorization, and nanotechnology. Yet, it remains unclear how enzyme propagation and substrate degradation interact, and especially whether and how enzymatic activity shapes the propagation process. Here, we bridge this gap by employing Fluorescence-Photon Correlation Imaging to simultaneously track directional enzyme propagation and biopolymer degradation in a model system. We use viscoelastic solutions of arabinoxylan, a hemicellulosic polysaccharide with a xylan backbone substituted by arabinose and ferulic acid, and a fluorescently labeled arabinoxylanase, an enzyme that randomly cleaves the xylan chain. To resolve enzyme propagation and biopolymer degradation with spatiotemporal precision, we combine fluorescence imaging of the enzyme with speckle-based photon correlation imaging, a technique to quantify biopolymer mobility, which we show is a proxy for biopolymer degradation. Our experiments reveal that enzyme diffusion is decoupled from catalytic activity, with no evidence of activity-enhanced diffusion. Instead, the progression of the degradation front is governed by a combination of enzyme diffusion, reaction kinetics, and slow enzyme deactivation, the latter being characterized by a double-exponential decay. By extending the Michaelis-Menten framework to space- and time-dependent conditions, we quantify how cumulative enzyme exposure and deactivation shape the degradation dynamics. This work establishes a quantitative framework to understand enzymatic processes in concentrated, beyond-dilute-regime substrates, with implications for the rationalization of biocatalytic systems in industrial and biomedical applications.
item.dc:creator: Vincenzo Ruzzi, Antoine Bouchoux, Carole Antoine-Assor, Donna-Joe Bigot, Salma Menzeh, Maike Petermann, Laurent Leclercq, Herv\'e Cottet, C\'edric Montanier, Claire Dumon, Luca Cipelletti, Laurence Ramos

item.title: Respiratory Mask Testing: Airway Inertance and System Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2610.04222v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Life support equipment coupled to the human lungs forms a complex, nonlinear dynamic system. Current respiratory mask test standards rely on sinusoidal breathing machines and surrogate trachea geometries that substantially reduce physiologically relevant airway inertance. This paper shows that the ISO 16900-5 trachea does not generate physiologically meaningful exhalation momentum, limiting the ability of standard test configurations to reveal valve dynamics relevant to human use. A physiologically motivated "lip-nozzle" surrogate is introduced as a diagnostic tool to restore representative momentum transfer, enabling observation of exhalation behavior that is not observable under existing test conditions. Nonlinear dynamic simulations incorporating this surrogate identify a force-balanced operating regime in which exhalation-jet momentum can offset flow-induced valve resistance. In one representative case, the exhalation mean effective pressure imposed on the wearer falls by approximately 85% and the flow work across the exhalation valve by approximately 92%. Because people do not exhale through a fully open mouth, this momentum is available in normal use. A valve aligned with the exhaled jet can recover part of the energy the wearer has already spent, rather than requiring additional effort. The magnitude of this effect depends on valve characteristics such as efficiency and the relationship between restoring force and lift, making it a design consideration for future valve development. Implications for mask design, valve placement, and future test methods are discussed. This work does not propose new performance limits or acceptance criteria; rather, it demonstrates how current test fixtures suppress inertance- and momentum-driven effects that can materially influence exhalation valve dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Mark M. Koeroghlian, Suraj Pawar, Raul G. Longoria
